subject: Accounting
title: Transfer Pricing Tricks
description: A quick win: understand Transfer Pricing Tricks.

hook.text: A tech company sells its own software to itself in Ireland—at a conveniently high price.

buildup.text: Transfer pricing is how companies set prices for transactions between their own subsidiaries.

discovery.text: By charging high prices to subsidiaries in high-tax countries, profits shift to low-tax ones.

twist.text: Tax authorities fight back with 'arm's length' rules—prices must match what unrelated parties would pay.

climax.text: Transfer pricing disputes cost governments billions and keep armies of tax lawyers employed.

punchline.text: Same company, different countries, different prices, lower taxes.

quiz.question: What is transfer pricing used for in tax avoidance?

details.summary: Transfer pricing is how multinational corporations set prices for transactions between their own subsidiaries in different countries. By charging inflated prices in high-tax countries, companies can shift profits to low-tax jurisdictions.
details.whyItMatters: Transfer pricing manipulation costs governments an estimated $500-600 billion annually and is the primary mechanism through which multinational corporations reduce their global tax bills.
takeaways: Transfer pricing governs how related companies in different countries price transactions between themselves
Companies can shift profits to low-tax countries by manipulating these internal prices
The arm's length principle requires internal prices to match what unrelated parties would charge

faq.question: How do companies use transfer pricing to reduce taxes?
faq.answer: A company can have its subsidiary in a tax haven charge inflated fees for intellectual property or services to its subsidiary in a high-tax country. The high-tax subsidiary's profits decrease (reducing taxes there), while profits accumulate in the low-tax haven where they're barely taxed.

faq.question: What is the arm's length principle?
faq.answer: It requires that transactions between related companies be priced as if they were between independent, unrelated parties. Tax authorities use this standard to detect artificial pricing. If a subsidiary pays 10x market rate for a service from a related company in a tax haven, that's a red flag.
